name: Lithuanian
variety: Standard Lithuanian (bendrinė kalba, based on the West Aukštaitian dialect of the Suvalkija region)
sources: Ambrazas, Vytautas (ed.) (1997). Lithuanian Grammar. Vilnius: Baltos lankos.
Pakerys, Antanas (1982). Lietuvių bendrinės kalbos prozodija. Vilnius: Mokslas.
Pakerys, Antanas (1995). Lietuvių bendrinės kalbos fonetika. Vilnius: Žara.
Girdenis, Aleksas (2014). Theoretical Foundations of Lithuanian Phonology. Vilnius. (English translation of Teoriniai lietuvių fonologijos pagrindai, 2nd edition 2003)
Dogil, Grzegorz (1999). Baltic languages. In H. van der Hulst (ed.), Word Prosodic Systems in the Languages of Europe. Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter.
Dogil, Grzegorz & Möhler, Gregor (1998). Phonetic invariance and phonological stability: Lithuanian pitch accents. Proceedings of ICSLP 98, Sydney.
Blevins, Juliette (1993). A tonal analysis of Lithuanian nominal accent. Language 69, 237-273.
Kenstowicz, Michael (1972). Lithuanian phonology. Studies in the Linguistic Sciences 2(2).
Mathiassen, Terje (1996). A Short Grammar of Lithuanian. Columbus, OH: Slavica.
Balode, Laimute & Holvoet, Axel (2001). The Lithuanian language and its dialects. In Ö. Dahl & M. Koptjevskaja-Tamm (eds.), The Circum-Baltic Languages, vol. 1. Amsterdam: John Benjamins.
contrasts: palatalised versus plain consonants throughout the system; the contrast is free before back vowels (spelled with i: kiaulė, liūtas) and automatic before front vowels
phonemic vowel length in stressed and unstressed syllables (y, į, ū, ų, ė, o, ą, ę are long)
acute versus circumflex syllable accent on long stressed syllables (áukštas 'tall' vs aũkštas 'storey'; šáuk 'shoot' vs šaũk 'shout')
position of stress is lexical and changes within paradigms (four accent classes of nouns)
mixed diphthongs: vowel plus l, m, n, r in one syllable behave like diphthongs and carry the accents
voiced versus voiceless obstruents (neutralised word-finally and in clusters); /f x ɣ/ occur only in loanwords
allophony: stressed short /ɐ ɛ/ are lengthened to [aː æː] with circumflex accent in most non-final syllables (nãmas [ˈnaːmɐs], gẽras [ˈɡʲæːrɐs])
every consonant before a front vowel is palatalised, and a cluster takes the palatalisation of its last member (kirsti)
vowels are fronted after palatalised consonants: /ɐ aː/ after a soft consonant are [ɛ æː] (written ia), /ʊ uː oː/ are fronted
word-final obstruents are devoiced before a pause (daug [dɐuk], kad [kɐt])
obstruent clusters take the voicing of their last member (dirbti [ˈdʲɪrʲpʲtʲɪ], atgal [ɐdˈɡɐɫ])
sibilant assimilation: s, z before č, dž become [ʃ ʒ]; identical consonants at a morpheme boundary merge into one (pusseserė)
hard /ɫ/ is velarised; /r/ is an alveolar trill; /ʋ/ is a weak labiodental
unstressed long vowels are shorter than stressed ones but keep their tense quality; short vowels are lax [ɪ ʊ ɛ ɐ]

in acute diphthongs and mixed diphthongs the first element is long and prominent (áu, ál, ár), except that short i, u stay short (ìl, ùr, ùi); in circumflex ones the second element, glide or sonorant, is lengthened (aũ, al̃, ar̃)
phonotactics: long syllables (long vowel, diphthong or vowel plus sonorant) carry the accent contrast; short stressed syllables have no contrast
no voiced obstruents before a pause
short /ɔ/ only in loanwords; native o is always long

stress.type: free (lexical), mobile, with pitch accent on long syllables
stress.rule: Stress can fall on any syllable and moves within paradigms according to the accent class of the word and the ending; ordinary spelling does not mark it. Dictionaries mark acute (´), circumflex (˜) and short stress (`).
stress.cues: duration and intensity first, pitch second; on long syllables the timing of the pitch and intensity peak distinguishes the two accents

rhythm.vowel_reduction: moderate: unstressed vowels are shortened and short unstressed vowels are lax, but length and quality contrasts are kept
rhythm.notes: The class label is an impression from the descriptive literature; no rhythm-metric study is cited.

length.notes: Long vowels are clearly longer than short ones, most of all under stress; unstressed long vowels are shortened. No exact ratio is quoted here (duration data are in Pakerys 1982). Diphthongs and mixed diphthongs count as long.

intonation.declarative: falling: pitch peaks on stressed syllables decline through the phrase, low ending
intonation.yes_no_question: often introduced by the particle ar; the pitch rises on the stressed syllable of the word in focus or at the end of the phrase
intonation.wh_question: high on the question word, then falling
intonation.continuation: rise at the end of a non-final phrase
intonation.accent_shape: pitch peak within the stressed syllable, early for acute and late for circumflex
intonation.notes: Sentence intonation is described only in general terms here (low confidence).

inventory.name: acute (tvirtapradė priegaidė), marked ´ (on i, u plus sonorant marked `)
inventory.description: falling: pitch and intensity peak early in the syllable; in diphthongs and mixed diphthongs the first element is long and tense (áu [âˑʊ])
inventory.phonation: modal; some laryngealisation is reported in dialects

inventory.name: circumflex (tvirtagalė priegaidė), marked ˜
inventory.description: level or rising: pitch and intensity peak late in the syllable; in diphthongs and mixed diphthongs the second element is lengthened and the first is short and reduced (aũ [ɒuˑ])

inventory.name: short stressed syllable, marked `
inventory.description: stressed short vowel; no accent contrast

tone.neutral_tone: unstressed syllables have no accent contrast in the standard language and follow the phrase contour
tone.notes: Chao numerals are a schematic rendering of the descriptions (Pakerys 1982; Dogil & Möhler 1998), not measured values. In the standard language the pitch difference between the accents is small; in diphthongs the contrast is carried mainly by the relative length and quality of the two elements, and in long monophthongs many speakers hardly distinguish the accents.

problems: No pitch accent: acute and circumflex are not distinguished, and accent marks in dictionary-style text are ignored (áukštas and aũkštas give the same output). A few suffix rules put the prominence on the first or second vowel of a diphthong (-áitis vs -aĩnis), which imitates the accents in those suffixes only.

Stress is penultimate by default, with some suffix rules; Lithuanian stress is lexical and mobile, so many words are wrong (žmogus, gerai, namai, vanduo, Lietuva, mokykla have final stress; vasara, ežeras have initial stress).
Hard l is defined as a vowel-type syllabic phoneme (IPA l̩, nominal length 300) and soft l carries the IPA label of a retroflex lateral (ɭ).
The diphthong ei is not recognised and is read as two vowels (sveiki [sʲvʲe.ˈɪ.kʲi]); iau is read as [e] plus [u] (kiaulė).

Soft labials, k, r and v are coded as consonant plus a palatal glide that is deleted before another consonant, so clusters lose palatalisation (kirsti); g, f, h, z, ž are never palatalised (geras, gėlė).

Devoicing before a voiceless consonant is overridden by the palatalisation rule when a front vowel follows the cluster (dirbti keeps [b]); final devoicing rules exist only for d, g, ž (final b, z stay voiced).
ę is a diphthong-like [ea] (phoneme eA) instead of [æː]; stressed a, e are not lengthened (namas, geras).
Only the default eSpeak tunes are used; wh-questions get the same fall-rise as yes-no questions.
good: phonemic vowel length from the spelling (y, į, ū, ų, ė, o, ą)
diphthongs ai, au, ui, ie, uo as single phonemes
palatalisation before front vowels and through clusters for t, d, s, š, n, l and the affricates
final devoicing of d, g, ž and voicing assimilation in simple clusters (daug, kad, bėgti, augti)

notes: No formant, VOT or rhythm-metric values are given because I cannot quote published figures with confidence.
